title: 𒋳𒈠 𒀀𒉿𒈝
titleEn: Laws of Hammurabi — §42–51: field and tenant (xii 63 – xiv 66)
part: Laws §42–51 · field and tenant (Col. xii 63 – xiv 66)
draftNote: The § chips number the laws (Harper’s sectioning, still standard); long laws span several tap-units. Readings checked sign-by-sign against Harper’s 1904 edition.
source: Louvre stele, after R.F. Harper, The Code of Hammurabi, King of Babylon (Chicago, 1904): transliteration and autograph plates, List of Signs. Readings are Harper’s in modern subscript notation. Cuneiform in Old Babylonian monumental sign forms via the SantakkuM webfont by Sylvie Vanséveren (CC BY 4.0); pronunciation: conventional reconstructed Old Babylonian. Audio: a German synthetic voice reads the Akkadian word by word from these pronunciation rules (word stress after Huehnergard). It cannot hold a consonant long, so doubled consonants are heard single (šumma with one m), and the emphatics ṭ and q are heard as plain t and k. Fresh translations made directly from the Akkadian; Harper’s public-domain translation consulted for sense only.

images.caption: The stele in the Louvre: a single block of black basalt about 2.25 m tall. In the relief at the top, Hammurabi stands before the enthroned sun-god Šamaš, the god of justice; the laws run in columns of cuneiform below.
images.alt: The tall black basalt stele of Hammurabi in a museum gallery, a relief of the king and the god Šamaš at its top
images.author: Enlil2

about: Ten laws on farmland worked by someone other than its owner, and on debts that a bad harvest makes unpayable. A tenant who grows nothing pays what his neighbour’s field yielded (§42); one who lets the field go to waste pays and puts it back in shape (§43); a man who took fallow land to break it in owes it ploughed and harrowed, plus a fixed rent, in the fourth year (§44). When the storm-god floods a rented field, who bears the loss depends on whether the rent was already paid or the harvest was to be shared (§45–46), and a tenant who fell behind may bring in another man to work the field (§47). Then the debtor: a flood or a drought year wipes out that year’s interest and suspends the debt (§48); a field pledged to a merchant is still harvested by its owner, who pays the merchant out of the crop — in grain or sesame at the king’s rates if he has no silver (§49–51).

sentences.i: If a man took a field on lease to cultivate and then grew no grain on it,
sentences.n: The tenant laws open. ana irrišūtim ušēṣi, “he brought (the field) out for cultivation,” is the leasing idiom: waṣûm “to go out” in the causative Š-stem, “to make go out.” uštabši is bašûm “to exist” in the causative Š-stem, perfect (the -ta- after the stem prefix, as in imtaḫar) — “he has caused to be,” i.e. he produced; you will meet it again at §49. Harper writes the field eqlam; the stele has the two signs A.ŠÀ, as everywhere in the code — Sumerograms read in Akkadian, as you have seen since §27.

sentences.i: he shall be proved to have done no work in the field, and he shall give the owner grain equal to what the neighbouring field yielded.
sentences.n: ina eqlim šiprim lā epēšim is a verbal noun phrase: “in the field, (of) work not doing” — the charge he is convicted on. ukannūšu is kânum in the D-stem, “they shall prove (it) against him,” the plural impersonal “they” of the court. kīma itêšu, “like its neighbour”: the rent is fixed by the yield of the field next door, so the owner loses nothing by the tenant’s idleness. Note the -ma chain again: ukannūšuma … inaddin, “they convict him, and (then) he gives.”

sentences.n: KI.KAL is uncultivated land: Harper’s sign list gives KI.KAL (he reads it KANKAL) as nidûtum, ground lying waste; later dictionaries read the logogram as kankallum, “hard, uncultivated land.” ana MU 3{kam}, “for three years,” uses the year-sign MU with the numeral three and the KAM marker you met in §30; read in Akkadian it is a plain count, šalāš šanātim (the spoken form is a reconstruction). aḫšu iddi, “he let his arm drop,” is the idiom for negligence. teptītum and iptete are both from petûm “to open”: virgin land is “opened.”

sentences.i: and he shall also measure out ten kor of grain for every ten bur of land.
sentences.n: A fixed rent for the wasted years. The literal word order is “and 10 GAN.E 10 ŠE.GUR”; the “for” is supplied. ŠE.GUR is grain by the kor (GUR, Harper: 300 KA, roughly 300 litres), and imaddad, from madādum, is “to measure out” grain — the code pays in barley as often as in silver. Harper reads both corner-wedges as the numeral ten and GAN.E as his GAN of 1,800 SAR, about 6⅔ acres (the unit later called the bur, būrum): “ten GUR per ten GAN.” Later study of the field-measure notation reads the first wedge differently: written before the field-sign it counts bur-units, so the line means “one bur,” and the rent is ten kor per bur — ten times Harper’s rate. The signs and the translation here follow Harper; the later reading is the one now generally accepted.

sentences.i: and afterwards the storm-god Adad flooded the field or a flood swept the crop away, the loss is the tenant’s.
sentences.n: {d}IM is Adad, the storm-god, written with the divine determinative and the sign IM (“storm”) — weather as an act of a god. irtaḫiṣ is raḫāṣum “to flood, wash over.” bibbulum is a crux: Harper takes it as “produce” (the god carried off the produce); later dictionaries read it as a flood (a high-water surge). The ending -um is nominative, which makes bibbulum the subject of itbal: “a flood carried (the crop) off.” Harper’s “produce” makes it the object instead, which the case ending does not support; we follow the flood reading, and the word itself remains rare. bitiqtum, “loss,” is a verbless clause: “the loss — of the tenant (it is),” the -ma on irrišimma stressing whose.

sentences.i: the tenant and the owner shall divide the grain that grows in the field in the agreed proportion.
sentences.n: Here the owner shares the storm’s damage: what is left is split. ibbaššû is the N-stem of bašûm with the subjunctive -û, “which comes to be.” ana apšitêm is a rare word and an honest uncertainty: Harper gives “agreement (?)” with his own question mark; the sense “according to the proportion (agreed)” comes from the context. izuzzū is zâzum, “to divide, share,” plural for the two parties.

sentences.i: If the tenant, because he did not get back his outlay in the previous year, has arranged for the field to be cultivated by another,
sentences.n: aššum “because.” mānaḫātum (plural of mānaḫtum) is the toil and outlay a man puts into land — here what he got back for it. The stele has an error in ilqû “he took”: the carver cut LU where QU was meant, il-LU-u; Harper prints il-lu(=qu)-u, keeping the stone and correcting it in parentheses, as he did at §32 and §34. eqlam erēšam iqtabi, literally “has spoken the field to be cultivated,” is compressed; we read it, with Harper, as arranging for someone else to farm it — a sublease. iqtabi is qabûm “to say” in the perfect.

sentences.n: irrissuma is irrišum + -šu “his tenant,” with the š of the suffix assimilated (irriš-šu → irrissu) and the -ma of emphasis: it is his (original) tenant who answers to him. sentences.i: If a man borrowed silver from a merchant and gave the merchant a field prepared for grain or sesame, telling him: “Cultivate the field, then harvest and take the grain or sesame that grows,”
sentences.n: A field pledged as security, with the creditor told to farm it himself. eqel epšētim is a field “of works,” already tilled and ready to sow. šamaššammū, sesame (the oil-plant), is written with three signs ŠE.GIŠ.Ì, “grain – wood – oil” (Harper’s ŠE.IZ.NI). erišma, esip, tabal are imperatives — direct speech quoted in the law, closed by iqbišum “he said to him.” Imperatives drop the prefix: erēšum → eriš “cultivate!”, esēpum → esip “gather!”, tabālum → tabal “take away!”

sentences.i: he shall give the merchant sesame at the going rate, according to the king’s schedule, for the silver and interest he borrowed from him.
sentences.n: Payment in kind when cash runs out — and the merchant may not set the price. maḫīrātišunu, “their rates”: maḫīrum is the market price. ana pî ṣimdat šarrim, literally “to the mouth of the king’s ordinance,” is the code’s phrase for an official tariff; pûm “mouth” is written with the KA sign. Harper renders ṣimdatum “scale”; it is the royal regulation, fixing the price. Harper prints il-ku-u in this line with a plain k where at XIV 40 he has il-qu-u: the stele has the same sign, KU (ku and qu), in both; the missing dot is a printing slip, and the word is ilqû “he took.”

glossary.-ma: and (clause-chaining particle); also “it is X that…”
glossary.10: ten — one corner-wedge (U); said ešret (?) with a masculine noun, ešer with a feminine one (Akkadian 3–10 take the opposite gender’s form): 10 ŠE.GUR “ten kor of grain”. Before a field-measure the wedge may count bur-units rather than tens (see §44)
glossary.3-kam: the 3rd; MU III{kam} “the third year” (KAM marks ordinals, as in §13) · also a plain count: ana MU 3{kam} “for three years”, said šalāš šanātim (spoken form reconstructed)
glossary.apāsum-D: D-stem (Harper’s apāsum II,1), a rare verb of uncertain meaning: ul uppas “he shall not object/interfere” — sense from context; Harper “interfere”
glossary.apšitûm: proportion, agreed share — uncertain and rare: Harper “agreement (?)”; apšitêm, ana apšitêm “in the (agreed) proportion”
glossary.awīlum: man; the free citizen, the code’s first legal class
glossary.aḫum: arm, side: aḫšu iddi “he let his arm drop” = he was idle, negligent
glossary.bašûm-Š: Š-stem of bašûm “to exist”: to bring into being, produce (a crop): uštabši “he has produced” (perfect)
glossary.bibbulum: flood, high water — uncertain: later dictionaries “flood”, Harper “produce”; bibbulum

glossary.ebūrum: harvest, the crop: ebūrim “of harvest, at harvest” (one logogram, read BURU₁₄; Harper writes ebûrim)

glossary.eqlum: field (written A.ŠÀ): eqelšu “his field” — the fief-land this whole block protects
glossary.erēšum: to ask, demand; also to cultivate: irriš “he demands (his field back)”
glossary.erēšum-N: N-stem of erēšum “to cultivate”: to be cultivated: inneriš “it was cultivated”
glossary.eršum: cultivated, sown: eqlam eršam “a sown field”
glossary.irrišum: tenant, cultivator: irrišum, ana irrišim “to a tenant”; irrissu “his tenant” (irriš + -šu; Harper reads the same spelling as a verb, “he shall cultivate it”)
glossary.irrišūtum: tenancy, cultivation on lease: ana irrišūtim “for cultivation (as a tenant)”
glossary.itûm: neighbour, the adjoining one: kīma itêšu “like its neighbour” (the neighbouring field)
glossary.išûm: to have: lā īšu “he has not”
glossary.kaspum: silver — the code’s money, written KÙ.BABBAR “shining precious-metal”
glossary.kurrum: the kor, a grain measure (written GUR; Harper: 300 KA): kur šeʾam “a kor of grain”
glossary.kânum-D: D-stem of kânum: to convict, prove against someone (uktīn, ukannūšuma)
glossary.lū: or; either (lū … lū “whether … or”); with verb: “let …”
glossary.madādum: to measure out (grain): imaddad “he shall measure out”
glossary.marārum: to hoe, break clods: imarrar “he shall hoe”
glossary.mayyārum: a tilling implement — uncertain: Harper “hoe”, later dictionaries a breaking-plough; mayyārī “with ploughs”
glossary.maḫrûm: first, former, previous: maḫrītim in šattim maḫrītim “in the previous year”
glossary.maḫāṣum: to strike; of ground, to break up: imaḫḫaṣ “he shall break up”
glossary.maḫīrum: market rate, price: ana maḫīrātišunu “at their rates”
glossary.mānaḫtum: toil, outlay, upkeep: mānaḫātišu “his upkeep (outlay)”; mānaḫat erēšim “the cost of cultivating”
glossary.nadûm: to cast, throw (a charge; a body into the river): iddi, nadû, iddû · also to leave lying (a field): ittadi “he has left (it) lying”
glossary.nadānum: to give, pay: inaddin, iddinam, iddinušum; nadānim “to give”
glossary.nidûtum: uncultivated, fallow land — Harper’s reading of KI.KAL (which he also gives as KANKAL); later dictionaries read the logogram as kankallum “hard, uncultivated land”
glossary.petûm: to open; of land, to bring into cultivation: iptete “he has opened”
glossary.pûm: mouth (the KA sign); ina pī mātim “in the mouth of the land” · ana pî ṣimdat šarrim “according to the mouth of the king’s ordinance”
glossary.qabûm: to speak, say: iqbû, iqtabi, iqabbûma
glossary.raḫāṣum: to flood, wash over: irtaḫiṣ “(Adad) has flooded”
glossary.raṭābum-D: D-stem of raṭābum “to be wet”: to moisten (a clay tablet, so it can be rewritten): uraṭṭab “he shall wet”; Harper reads u-ra-ad-da-ab
glossary.rebûm: fourth: rebûtim šattim “in the fourth year”
glossary.tabālum: to take away, carry off: itabbal · tabal “take!” (imperative)
glossary.tamkārum: merchant (written tam-KAR §32, DAM.GÀR §40): the ransom-fronting, land-buying businessman of the code
glossary.teptītum: opening-up, bringing waste land into cultivation: teptītim “for opening-up”
glossary.târum-D: D-stem of târum: to give back: turru “taken away/captured”; utarrūšumma “they shall return (it) to him”
glossary.waṣûm-Š: Š-stem of waṣûm “to go out”: to send out, bring out; of land, to take on lease: ana irrišūtim ušēṣi “he took (a field) for cultivation”
glossary.zâzum: to divide, share: izuzzū “they shall divide”
glossary.šaluštum: one-third: šalušti eqlim “a third of the field” — the widow’s child-raising portion · also a third of the crop in a sharecrop lease: šaluš
glossary.šamaššammū: sesame, the oil-plant: šamaššammam, šamaššammim (written ŠE.GIŠ.Ì; Harper ŠE.IZ.NI)
glossary.šarrum: king: šarrum “the king”, šar-ri-im “of the king”
glossary.šumma: if — the word that opens every law of the code
glossary.ḫubullum: debt, an interest-bearing loan: ḫubullum; bēl ḫubullim “the creditor”
glossary.ṣimdatum: royal ordinance, regulation: ṣimdat šarrim “the king’s ordinance” (Harper: “scale”)
glossary.ṭuppum: the clay tablet; the deed: ṭuppašu iḫḫeppi “his tablet shall be smashed” — the sale annulled physically
